title: Optimizing Large-Array Workloads
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of optimizing large-array workloads and name one situation where it is useful.
Apply chunked computation to a small NumPy example and inspect the resulting values, shape, or dtype.
Identify one important limitation, boundary case, or validation check for optimizing large-array workloads.

content.intro: This lesson develops topic 179 of the supplied curriculum: **Optimizing Large-Array Workloads**. The main starting point is **Chunked computation**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Views and references can share memory, while copies own separate data. Awareness of this difference prevents accidental mutation and helps explain memory/performance trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Optimizing Large-Array Workloads** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Chunked computation** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.arange(10)
chunk_sums = [int(chunk.sum()) for chunk in np.array_split(values, 3)]
print(chunk_sums, sum(chunk_sums))

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a slice owns independent memory
common_mistakes.why: Basic slicing commonly creates a view.
Short timings vary due to startup, cache, and system noise.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat measurements, use representative sizes, and compare equivalent work.
